paragraphs: No free communities have ever existed without morals, and, as I observed in the earlier part of this work, morals are the work of woman. Whatever affects the condition of women, their habits and their opinions, therefore has great political importance in my eyes. Among almost all Protestant nations, young women are far more in charge of their own actions than they are in Catholic countries. This independence is greater still in Protestant countries like England, which have kept or gained the right of self-government; there, political habits and religious opinions bring the spirit of freedom into the domestic circle. In the United States, the doctrines of Protestantism are joined with great political freedom and a most democratic state of society, and nowhere are young women left so early or so completely to their own guidance. Long before an American girl reaches marriageable age, her release from her mother’s control begins. She has hardly stopped being a child when she already thinks for herself, speaks freely and acts on her own impulse. The great scene of the world lies constantly open before her. Far from being hidden from her, it is shown to her more fully every day, and she is taught to look at it with a steady and calm gaze. So the vices and dangers of society are revealed to her early. She sees them clearly, looks at them without illusions and faces them without fear, for she is full of reliance on her own strength, and everyone around her seems to share that reliance. An American girl almost never shows the virginal bloom amid youthful desires, or the innocent, artless grace that usually accompanies the European woman in the passage from girlhood to youth. It is rare for an American woman, at any age, to show childish timidity or ignorance. Like the young women of Europe, she wants to please, but she knows exactly what pleasing costs. If she does not give herself up to evil, at least she knows that it exists, and she is notable more for purity of conduct than for chastity of mind. I have often been surprised, and almost alarmed, by the remarkable skill and happy boldness with which young women in America manage their thoughts and their words through all the difficulties of a stimulating conversation. A philosopher would have stumbled at every step along the narrow path they walked without accident and without effort. It is easy to see that even in the independence of early youth, an American woman is always mistress of herself. She enjoys every permitted pleasure without surrendering to any of them, and her reason never lets the reins of self-guidance fall, though it often seems to hold them loosely.

In France, the opinions and tastes of the people still mix the remnants of every age in strange ways. There, women commonly receive a reserved, secluded and almost cloistered education, as they did in aristocratic times, and then they are suddenly left, without a guide and without help, amid all the irregularities that cannot be separated from democratic society. The Americans are more consistent. They have discovered that in a democracy the independence of individuals cannot fail to be very great, youth premature, tastes poorly restrained, customs fleeting, public opinion often unsettled and powerless, paternal authority weak and marital authority contested. In these circumstances, they believed they had little chance of suppressing the most violent passions of the human heart in woman, and they concluded that the surer way was to teach her the art of fighting those passions herself. Since they could not keep her virtue from being exposed to frequent danger, they resolved that she should know how best to defend it. They placed more trust in the free vigor of her will than in safeguards that have been shaken or overthrown. Instead of teaching her to distrust herself, then, they constantly try to build up her confidence in her own strength of character. Because it is neither possible nor desirable to keep a young woman in perpetual or complete ignorance, they hurry to give her early knowledge on every subject. Far from hiding the corruptions of the world from her, they would rather she saw them at once and trained herself to avoid them, and they think it more important to protect her conduct than to be overly scrupulous about her innocence.

The Americans are a very religious people, yet they do not rely on religion alone to defend a woman’s virtue; they also try to arm her reason. In this they follow the same method as in several other matters. They first make the most vigorous efforts to get individual independence to exercise proper control over itself, and they do not call on the aid of religion until they have reached the utmost limits of human strength. I am aware that an education of this kind is not without danger. I realize that it tends to strengthen the judgment at the expense of the imagination, and to produce cold and virtuous women rather than affectionate wives and agreeable companions for men. Society may be calmer and better regulated, but domestic life often has fewer charms. These, however, are secondary evils, which can be faced for the sake of higher interests. At the stage we have now reached, the time for choosing is no longer in our hands. A democratic education is indispensable to protect women from the dangers that democratic institutions and mores place around them.
